title: Retrieve, stuff or cache? Then cite it and debug it
brief: The corpus fits in a context window. Or nearly does. Or it fits for one user and not for another. Retrieval is no longer the only way to put knowledge in a prompt, and whichever you pick, a bad answer still needs a debugging path and every claim needs a source.

blocks.text: Three ways to put knowledge in front of the model

blocks.title: RAG, long context, CAG and routing
blocks.intro: Li et al. found that when resourced enough, long-context models beat RAG on average, but RAG is much cheaper [[r21]]. Accuracy also falls as input grows: in NoLiMa, 11 of 13 models fell below half of their short-context baseline at 32K tokens, and GPT-4o dropped from 99.3% to 69.7% [[r23]]. Chroma's report of 2025-07-14 saw 18 LLMs become less reliable as input grew [[r25]].

options.name: RAG
options.summary: Retrieve a few chunks per query.
cons: Retrieval can miss, so recall and abstention need work
More components to run and evaluate
options.bestWhen: The corpus is large, changes often or has per-user permissions.
options.avoidWhen: The corpus is tiny and static, where an index adds only risk.

options.name: Long context per query
options.summary: Put the whole corpus, or a large slice, into every prompt.
pros: Best accuracy on average in Li et al. when resourced enough
cons: Per-query cost grows with corpus size
Evidence in the middle is used less (Lost in the Middle)
Accuracy degrades with length and distractors
options.bestWhen: The corpus is small. Anthropic's rule of thumb is under 200,000 tokens, about 500 pages.
options.avoidWhen: The corpus is larger than the window or the cost per query matters.

options.name: Cache-augmented generation (CAG)
options.summary: Preload a small, manageable corpus into the context and cache the runtime KV state, so no retrieval runs per query.
pros: Lower latency and no retrieval errors for constrained knowledge bases, as the paper claims
Simplest serving path for a shared, static corpus
cons: Not suited to large or fast-changing corpora
One cached state cannot hide documents per user (a reasoned limit, not a quote from the paper)
options.bestWhen: A small, stable, shared knowledge set serves many queries.
options.avoidWhen: Access differs per user or content changes every day.

options.name: Route per query (Self-Route)
options.summary: Try RAG first and send the query to long context only if the model judges the retrieved evidence insufficient.
pros: Keeps accuracy near long context at lower cost
cons: Two paths to build, secure and evaluate
The long-context fallback must fit the data it needs
options.bestWhen: Most queries are easy and a few need the whole picture.
options.avoidWhen: You cannot afford to maintain two paths.

blocks.title: RAG, long context or CAG?
blocks.prompt: Flip the corpus size, the change rate and the permission model.

options.name: Long context per query
options.summary: Stuff the corpus into every prompt.

fits.why: It works, with more moving parts than the corpus needs.

big.why: Retrieval is the only way when the corpus is far larger than the window.

peruser.why: Permission filters trim results per caller.

fits.why: No index to build, and long context beat RAG on average when resourced enough.

stable.why: You pay for the whole corpus on every query unless the prefix is cached.

fast.why: No index to refresh, so new documents go straight into the prompt.

peruser.why: You can build each prompt from the caller's visible documents, but prefixes cannot be shared across users.

fits.why: A small, manageable knowledge set is its intended use.

big.why: It cannot preload what does not fit.

fast.why: The cache must be rebuilt whenever knowledge changes.

peruser.why: One cached state cannot hide documents per user.

fits.why: RAG first and long context for hard queries costs less than long context alone.

big.why: The long-context fallback needs a large slice of the corpus to fit.

stable.why: Both paths are simple on stable data.

fast.why: The RAG leg stays fresh, but you run two paths.

peruser.why: Both paths must enforce the filter, which doubles the places to get it wrong.

blocks.takeaway: Permissions and change rate usually decide before accuracy does. A shared cache is the first thing per-user access breaks.

Anthropic `citations` on `document` or `search_result` blocks return `char_location`, `page_location` or `content_block_location` spans, and `cited_text` does not count toward output tokens [[r27]]. OpenAI file search in the Responses API returns `file_citation` annotations [[r30]]
That the cited span entails the claim
Anthropic citations with structured outputs returns HTTP 400. OpenAI raw hits come back only with `include: ["file_search_call.results"]`
For documents over 20k tokens, ask for word-for-word quotes, then answer from them [[r41]]
That the quotes are used faithfully
A second step adds latency and tokens
An entailment model or judge checks each claim against its cited span
Another model call, covered in the guardrails world

blocks.title: Debug a bad answer from the bottom up

steps.title: In the corpus?
steps.md: Is the answer text in an indexed chunk? Check ingestion and parsing first.

steps.title: Retrieved?
steps.md: Is the gold chunk in the candidate set? Measure recall@k before reranking.

steps.title: Kept?
steps.md: Did fusion, the reranker and the cutoff keep it? Compare its rank at each stage.

steps.title: In the prompt?
steps.md: Is it present, untruncated and well placed in the final prompt?

steps.title: Used?
steps.md: Did the model use it and cite a span that supports the claim?

items.symptom: A confident answer cites a chunk that is irrelevant.
items.cause: A retrieval miss with no abstention gate.
items.fix: Check candidate recall and the cutoff, then add an abstention rule.

items.symptom: The fact exists in the corpus and is never retrieved.
items.cause: The chunking split it, an identifier needs a keyword leg, or the query and page share no vocabulary.
items.fix: Find the chunk that holds the fact, then add BM25, a rewrite or a different chunk boundary.

items.symptom: The gold chunk sits at fused rank 31 and is absent from the prompt.
items.cause: Candidates were cut before the reranker, or the reranker only sees the top 50.
items.fix: Raise recall, rerank a deeper list, and log the rank at every stage.

items.symptom: The gold chunk is in the prompt and the answer ignores it.
items.cause: Position and length effects: evidence in the middle of a long context is used least.
items.fix: Send fewer, better-ranked chunks with the strongest first or last.

items.symptom: The answer cites a source that does not support the claim.
items.cause: A citation proves provenance, not entailment.
items.fix: Add quote-first prompting or a support check on each claim.

items.cause: Ingestion lag, an old index version or a cache that outlived the content.
items.fix: Compare document timestamps in the prompt with the source, and check cache TTLs.

items.symptom: A list-everything question returns an incomplete list.
items.cause: Top-k limits what one retrieval can return.
items.fix: Decompose, use a summary or graph index, or raise k with a cap.

blocks.title: What interviewers listen for
blocks.md: They ask where you would look first for a wrong answer. A strong answer walks the stages in order, names the metric at each (recall@k, rank after rerank, prompt contents, support rate) and says which log line proves it.

quiz.q: A 150,000-token corpus is placed in every prompt with no caching. A RAG pipeline sends 6,000 tokens per query. At the same price per input token, how many times more input cost does long context carry per query?
quiz.explain: 150,000 / 6,000 = 25, so each long-context query carries 25 times the input tokens. Prompt caching can shrink the gap and long context can be more accurate, so the real decision also weighs accuracy, update rate and permissions.

quiz.q: A team proposes cache-augmented generation for HR policies, where each employee may see a different subset. Which statement is correct?
options: CAG works because a cached prefix is filtered per user at generation time
CAG removes retrieval errors for every corpus, so permissions stop mattering
One cached context cannot hide documents per user, so use filtered retrieval or per-user prompts
CAG needs a vector index, so it cannot be used with HR policies at all
quiz.explain: A cached context is shared state, so every user would see every preloaded document. Per-user visibility needs filtering before documents enter the context, which means filtered retrieval or a per-user prompt. The cache is not filtered at generation time, the claim about every corpus overreaches, and CAG needs no vector index.

quiz.q: The retrieval log below ends in a wrong answer. What is the best first change?

code.code:
gold chunk: C17
rank after rerank: 3
chunks in prompt: 20, with C17 at position 11
answer: ignores C17 and cites C4

options: Raise k to 40 so that more of the relevant evidence is present in the prompt
Send fewer chunks and put the strongest at the start or end
Switch to a larger embedding model so retrieval ranks the chunk even higher
Add a BM25 leg to the retriever so identifiers are matched exactly
quiz.explain: The retriever already ranked C17 third, so recall and ranking worked. The failure is position and volume: evidence in the middle of a long context is used least. A larger k adds more distractors, a bigger embedding model changes retrieval, and a BM25 leg addresses a miss that did not happen.

quiz.q: Select every true statement about Anthropic's Citations feature and citations in general.
options: Enabling citations together with structured outputs returns HTTP 400
A citation proves the cited span supports the claim
quiz.explain: The docs say citations and structured outputs together return HTTP 400, and list the three location types. `cited_text` is not counted toward output tokens. A citation shows where text came from, not that the claim follows from it, which is why a separate support check exists.

takeaways: RAG, long context and CAG differ on corpus size, change rate and permissions more than on accuracy
A shared cached context cannot enforce per-user access
Debug in stage order: corpus, candidates, ranking, prompt, answer
A citation proves provenance, not entailment
